Chapter 11: The Fragility of Systems Without Skin in the Game.
You know, it’s so tempting to look at massive organizations—governments, big corporations, huge institutions—and assume they’re strong just because they’re big. But here’s the thing: size can be really misleading.
If the people running those systems don’t actually have skin in the game, even the biggest, toughest-looking structures can turn out to be brittle, or even ready to crumble at the worst moment.
Picture this: there’s a bridge in your town, but it was designed by engineers who never actually cross it, built by a contractor from miles away, and maintained by workers who don’t even live nearby. If something goes wrong, who really feels the consequences? Not those who made the decisions. To everyone else, the bridge looks solid—but underneath, it’s just waiting for a problem.
And it’s not just bridges. This same pattern pops up everywhere. Think about financial systems run by folks with no personal stake, or healthcare managed by distant administrators, or education policies made by people who’ve never set foot in the classroom. What do these have in common? When mistakes happen, the pain is so spread out that nobody learns quickly, and real accountability disappears.
There’s a story from aviation that really drives this home. Imagine an airline outsourcing its maintenance to a company far away. The workers get paid by the hour; they don’t know the passengers and probably never will. If there’s a mistake, the fallout can be catastrophic—but those who made the call are nowhere near the mess. The whole system was built to be efficient, but in reality, it’s dangerously fragile.
Most of us don’t realize just how much of our daily lives rest on these systems that lack real, personal accountability. That’s why small errors sometimes spiral into disasters, and why trust is so easily broken.
But here’s the good news—there are ways to make systems stronger. It really comes down to one thing: making sure the people who make the decisions are also exposed to the results, good or bad. When pilots, engineers, or managers actually share in the risks, they’re more careful, more invested, and way more responsive. The system gets stronger—not because it’s bigger, but because everyone involved takes responsibility.
So, what’s the takeaway? Size alone isn’t enough. Real strength comes from having skin in the game—from being willing to bear the cost of failure, and to grow from it. That’s how systems become truly robust, adaptable, and worthy of our trust.
